comments.text: I'm tired of hearing about teachers low salaries. Perhaps it's so in certain parts of the country but where I am, teachers can do quite well. You don't earn much at first but your salary grows over time. Your job security builds with time as well regardless of how good or bad an educator you are, thanks to the union protections. If you earn your Masters Degree you'll see a significant bump in pay (many in this school district make six figures). If you stick with this profession and make it a career you could potentially end up with a very lucrative pension. How many professions out there can boast about a pension? Fewer and fewer. Also, there is a tremendous amount of time off. Granted, you must take the time off when the students are off, but it is time off, nevertheless. Combined with nearly two months off for summer vacation you still have the option to work part time to bolster your income. The teaching profession accounts for one of the highest percentage rates of millionaires in retirement. Think about that.

comments.author: @frodrickfronkensteen9241
comments.text:
For a single person (young or old), perhaps a widow(er) or somebody with no family ... CDL driving is viable way to earn a living.
For a person with a family, it can more challenging.
For a married couple, both willing and able to enter life on the road, look into it. "Team" Driving can be profitable and rewarding.
For a person who is down on their luck/a day away from the streets, CDL driving can be a lifeline and possibly a new start on life ...

During the first year (typically an Over The Road (OTR) driving job), most can quite literally live out of their company-provided trucks. It's a large closet w/no bathroom, but the mortgage/rent payment is $0 per month. Laundry and biology needs are met at truck stops, gyms and your company's terminal. It's the opposite of a pampered existence, but hardy and/or determined folks CAN hang in there and assimilate to the lifestyle.

Do your research (<read that again) on companies to start with. There are predatory starter companies that should be avoided. There ARE decent ones.
There are predatory "Lease" agreements, where predators paint it as an "Owner/Operator" opportunity, which it IS NOT. Do not get talked into a lease by a starter company.
Be cautious about signing contracts where a starter company offers "FREE!" CDL training. Complete the "contract" year, and you're good. If you quit, you pay, BIG TIME$$$. Research!!!

Get your CDL, your training and your first year of experience, and real pay and a myriad of driving options present themselves, apart from OTR driving jobs.
Get 30 months of experience, keep a clean driving record/no accidents, and you have job options that offer six figures, benefits, PTO, etc.

comments.author: @displacedtexan8953
comments.text:
Just watching the parts of the video about nursing. I was a new graduate nurse recruiter in the Las Vegas area. I covered 4 hospitals in Vegas and 2 in California. One of the hospitals I worked at in Cali was in San Jose. Nurses there made a ton on paper. The cost of living there is insane. That being said...For reference purposes when I posted a position I would have literally 50-100 new grad applicants per position. When we had job fairs at the hospitals we would easily have 100-150 new grad nurses show up. Usually we would have 15-20 jobs total for each hospital. I recruited 20-30 new grad nurses for each hospital about every quarter. Usually I was handling 100-120 new grad nurses resumes per quarter. 

If there are any new graduate nurses on here reading this, some advice from a new grad nurse recruiter from a MAJOR hospital chain...get your foot in the door in whichever department offers you a position. Once you have experience it is way easier to move around- especially at a large hospital. You make connections. You prove yourself. You get to the department you want. There are very few openings in the ER and labor and delivery.
